INTERVENORS DEBORAH NOBLES’ AND GERALD C. NOBLES, JR.’s
INDIVIDUALLY AND AS REPRESENTATIVES OF L BAR FAMILY RANCH, LP’S INITIAL BRIEF

	
COME NOW, Deborah Nobles and Gerald C. Nobles, Jr., Individually and as Representatives of the L Bar Family Ranch, LP., Intervenors (Party Number 625) in above PUC and SOAH Document numbers, respectfully files this Initial Brief in opposition to any route using Links M22 and K51.     In support of this Response, Intervenors Deborah Nobles, Gerald C. Nobles, Jr., and L Bar Family Ranch LP. would respectfully show the following.

INTRODUCTION
As only a brief summary, much of the testimony and cross-examination in the Hearing on Merits was intended to protect various landowner routes and links, using only small portions of the  routes and links, without further examining  the entire length of their specific routes or links.  Specifically, Deborah Nobles, Gerald C. Nobles, Jr., and L Bar Family Ranch, LP. uses the following Brief segments to validate their opposition to Links M22 and K51 being selected.

DISRUPTION OF CURRENT AND FUTURE RIVER RANCHING OPERATION
 Examining the Applicants’ maps, route M22 runs closely east/west parallel to the San Saba River bisecting the River Ranch toward both the home and Bed & Breakfast facility of the ranch.  Then, M22 continues northwest, continuing the bisection,2 destroys the functionality of the ranch, and crosses the Hickory water well, large storage tank, and water troughs watering all the livestock and wildlife on the majority of the high fence portion of the ranch.1 
 This M22 Link destroys the current use of the operations of the ranch.  With a great reduction or possibly eliminating prescribed burns of brush and pastureland,2 grass management is eliminated, eventually  reducing stocking  rates. Couple this with  both  the disruption of current pastures and water availability to livestock and wildlife, the cow/calf, horse, and wildlife capabilities would be severely limited. Now creating reduction of animals and no future for  growth.
The Bed and Breakfast facility would suffer greatly from the close 765 kV transmission line view, entering, exiting, and at the premises. Bed and Breakfast facility usage would drop dramatically.
The River Ranch’s wildlife hunting would greatly decrease with exotic hunting lessees and other hunting enthusiasts leaving immediately.3 These hunters, who brought in new 
Testimony, PUC Item 3726, pg. 5 and exhibits 1a, 1b, 1c, 1d
HOM Transcripts, Vol. 3. pg. 127
HOM Transcripts, Vol. 3, pg. 67 

whitetail genetics and new exotic species, took decades to develop.
Helicopter use for hog hunting and TP&W wildlife management permit counting would be eliminated. Future growth is eliminated.
The planned airstrip for both hunting and bed and breakfast use would be eliminated. With no physical inspection,4 applicants are unaware that their link crosses the only possible landscape location for an airstrip. Future growth terminated.
The value of the entire bisected ranch as a whole would be decimated for perpetuity. 
VOCA RANCH DISRUPTION
The K51 Link on the Voca Ranch is still located in the corridor of the San Saba River corridor.  Running this huge transmission line along a high ridge on the north fence from east to west, the ridge becomes an aesthetic nightmare for miles east and west from the south.  Any movement of the transmission line to the south encounters four large irrigated pivots, then hunting lodge, next a ranch home, then barns, pens, and arenas prior to creeks entering the San Saba River.5
	In his rebuttal of Jason Buntz, Luther King, largest landowner in McCulloch County, expressed that through his vast lifelong experience a longer route, preferably to the north, would be more advantageous.6 In cross-examination, he again emphasized a more northern route would be preferable than river corridor property.7 Note that he did not specifically mention the proposed
routes north suggested by the Applicants.  Mr. King’s expert, Jim Scott, actually favors expanding 
the study area further north.8
HOM Transcripts, Vol. 3, pg.1125 and Vol. 4, pg. 157-159
Testimony, PUC Item 3726, pg. 5 and exhibits 2a, 2b
Testimony, PUC Item 5026, pg. 1 – 4
HOM Transcripts, Vol. 6, pg. 100 -101
Testimony, PUC Item 4507, pg. 13, 14

FLOODING AND PROPERTY DEVASTATION
Flooding and massive destruction of property needs to be actually seen and not just read 
about.9 The McCulloch County Commissioners tried to explain the severity of these issues, but were limited due to Applicants’ objections.10 Additionally, Bruce James and myself were not permitted to cross examine one another concerning the flooding and access destruction. To experience “hands on” frightened summer vacationers be stranded and emergency evacuated was traumatic.  To experience the destruction of land and vegetation hundreds of yards wide for miles along the San Saba River was sobering. For your wife to be stranded on the ranch for 21 days with no exit possible in any direction, and not being able to receive mail, buy groceries, etc., is a true hardship.11   
The intersection of L2, L4, M21, M22 is a notorious example of the Flash Flood Alley of the San Saba River.12   With numerous creeks entering the river and growing in strength as they enter the river, the devastation is horrific.  County roads are completely destroyed with good repairs being untimely and potential for heavy traffic not possible.13 What will the utility companies do when access for an emergency is unavailable for their easement?
At the intersection of the San Saba River and L4, Route 296 proposes to join another AEP transmission line within 150 feet to cross the San Saba River.  Just previously noted, this is a poor location much less joining another transmission line at a river crossing, creating “a single point of failure.”14 Paralleling another transmission line is mostly advantageous except at 

HOM Transcript, Vol. 3, pg. 114-116; Vol. 4, pg. 141; Vol. 4, pg. 182-184; Vol. 4, pg. 186-190 
HOM Transcript, Vol. 6, pg. 205-214; Vol. 6, pg. 219-224
Testimony PUC Item 3726, pg.4, 5 and exhibits 1e, 1f; Sup Testimony PUC Item 3857, pg. 3, 4, 5
HOM Transcript, Vo. 4, pg. 184; Vol. 4, pg. 188
See #10 Above
 HOM Transcript, Vol. 4, pg. 184; Reb Testimony PUC Item 5052, pg. 15
crossings.15   However, the paralleling the river is a different matter.  At this intersection, Route 296 travels closely to the San Saba River for many miles both to the east and west  from this flash flood alley intersection, creating more potential flooding problems for the utilities, the counties, and the landowners. Not only does the binary system not work for habitations, but river crossings should be questioned for severity, and not just another river crossing.16
ROUTE COMPARISONS
Route 296 is inferior in the many ways previously covered. As for route CCG, Will McAdams comparison is a full route thorough comparison including CCG.17  Plus, why propose a route to go further deeper and closer along the San Saba River. 
vi.	CLOSING REMARKS
	As a past president of the National Ranching Heritage Association,18 I have defended the ranching community and helped educate thousands of adults and children on the history and necessity of the vast ranching industry. My heart aches especially at the destruction of historic ranches and lifelong dreams of ranching heritage families whose properties are greatly harmed forever for future generations.  And now, I am one of these. Of all the participants in these proceedings, the landowners have the most to lose. I urge you to slow down and listen to the Texas lawmakers as to updated current and alternative needs.
HOM Transcript, Vol. 4, pg. 217-218; Vol. 4, pg. 188-189
